text: Collaborate and Promote Visibility asks organizations to work together across boundaries, rather than letting each team optimize only within its own function. A network team can hit its own SLA while a customer-facing incident drags on, because nobody owns the end-to-end picture across the boundary. This principle specifically targets that natural pull toward silos — not generic advice to communicate more.

Visibility is what makes collaboration achievable in practice. Work and its outcomes need to be visible to the people who need to see them, not buried in one team's private queue. When the state of a change or incident is genuinely visible, people act on accurate information. When it's hidden, even well-intentioned collaboration breaks down, because people are working from different, outdated pictures of what's actually happening.

One reliable symptom this principle is being ignored: the same question gets three different answers in three different meetings, because each team has its own private version of the current state. Another: a change gets approved without the downstream team, who'll actually be affected, ever hearing about it until it breaks something.

Collaboration doesn't mean involving everyone in everything — over-including people wastes time just as badly as leaving them out. The real judgment call is identifying who's actually affected or has relevant knowledge, and bringing them in at the point their input genuinely changes the outcome, not as a courtesy afterthought.
Cross the boundaries, make the work visible, involve the right people early. Next up: the final three guiding principles together — Think Holistically, Keep It Simple, and Optimize and Automate.
